q.intro.text: This U S G S map of Alaska is marked one to sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty. The straight line from the trailhead to the lake is two and a half inches long on the map. How far is it on the ground? Pick an answer, and say how sure you are.

e.intro.text: Four steps. Press each one: the map and the lines move first, then the notation.

e.step0.text: One to sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty has no units, so both sides use the same unit. Measure in inches: one inch on the map stands for sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty inches on the ground.

e.step1.text: The line is two and a half inches, so the ground is two and a half times sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty: one hundred fifty-eight thousand, four hundred inches. True, but who measures a trail in inches?

e.step2.text: Pick a unit that fits a trail. Divide by twelve: thirteen thousand, two hundred feet. Divide by five thousand, two hundred eighty: two and a half miles.

e.step3.text: Look: two and a half inches on the map, two and a half miles on the ground. No accident. Five thousand, two hundred eighty times twelve is sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty, so that many inches make exactly one mile. One to sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty is the same as one inch to one mile.

e.why.text: Quick check: why is one to sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty the same as one inch to one mile?

e.why.ok.text: Yes. A mile is sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty inches, and the scale pairs inches with inches.

e.why.ft.text: A mile is five thousand, two hundred eighty feet. The sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty are inches, the same unit as the map inch.

e.why.cm.text: Ratio scales work in any unit. Here: inches on the map, inches on the ground.

t.intro.text: Your turn. A U S G S topo map is one to twenty-four thousand. From the parking lot to the summit is three and a half inches on the map. Step one is done for you.

t.mul.text: Three and a half times twenty-four thousand is how many inches? Tip: three and a half times twenty-four first, then times one thousand.

t.mul.whole.text: Seventy-two thousand is three times twenty-four thousand. The half inch counts too: half of twenty-four thousand more.

t.mul.pow.text: Check the size. Three times twenty-four thousand is seventy-two thousand, and four times is ninety-six thousand. The answer is in between.

t.mul.no.text: Split it: three and a half times twenty-four is eighty-four, then times one thousand.

t.mul.ok.text: Yes. Three and a half times twenty-four is eighty-four, and eighty-four times one thousand is eighty-four thousand inches.

t.ft.text: Eighty-four thousand inches is hard to picture. How many feet is that?

t.ft.same.text: That is still inches. Twelve inches make one foot: divide by twelve.

t.ft.times.text: Feet are bigger than inches, so there are fewer of them. Divide.

t.ft.mi.text: That divides by five thousand, two hundred eighty, as if the inches were feet. Inches to feet first: divide by twelve.

t.ft.no.text: Eighty-four thousand divided by twelve is how many?

t.ft.ok.text: Yes. Eighty-four thousand divided by twelve is seven thousand feet. Printed on every U S G S topo map: one inch is two thousand feet.

t.size.text: Is seven thousand feet a short walk or a long hike? A mile is five thousand, two hundred eighty feet.

t.size.ok.text: Yes. Seven thousand divided by five thousand, two hundred eighty is about one point three miles. Feet or miles both work; miles are easier to picture.

t.size.sixteen.text: Sixteen comes from eighty-four thousand divided by five thousand, two hundred eighty: inches treated as feet. Seven thousand feet is just over a mile.

t.size.half.text: Half a mile is two thousand, six hundred forty feet. Seven thousand feet is more than a whole mile.

q.cb.right.text: At the start you picked two and a half miles, and you were right. Now you can show why: sixty-three thousand, three hundred sixty inches make a mile.

q.cb.ft.text: At the start you picked one hundred fifty-eight thousand, four hundred feet. Those were inches: the scale pairs inches with inches.

q.cb.thirty.text: At the start you picked thirty miles. That skipped inches to feet: divide by twelve first, then by five thousand, two hundred eighty.

q.cb.none.text: Same unit on both sides, multiply, then pick a unit that fits. That works for every ratio scale.

p.intro.text: Jo puts a straight six thousand foot trail on the one to twenty-four thousand map. Six thousand divided by twenty-four thousand is one quarter, so it is a quarter inch long. Is Jo right?

p.test.text: Let's test it. Build the argument, and see where it leads.

p.build.text: Now prove it. Fill each because with the reason that makes the line true.

p.no.times.text: Multiplying makes it twenty-four thousand times longer than the real trail. Ground to map shrinks: divide.

p.no.units.text: They matter. One to twenty-four thousand means inches with inches. The feet must become inches first.

p.no.other.text: True, but it is the reason for a different line. Which reason makes this line true?

p.c1.text: Right. Jo mixed units: feet on the ground, inches on the map.

p.c2.text: Right. Six thousand times twelve is seventy-two thousand inches.

p.c3.text: Right. Seventy-two thousand divided by twenty-four thousand is three inches. Jo's line was twelve times too short.

p.done.text: That's a proof: three claims, each with its reason, and the lines back every one. Change the ground to the map's unit first, then divide.
